title: Morning Edition
notes: It prioritizes developments since Thursday’s morning and evening editions: Microsoft’s outage running into a second day, the Kremlin saying it has not yet agreed to European mediators, China ruling out hosting COP33, Chris Van Hollen’s challenge to Chuck Schumer, and Manchester United’s reported deal for USA coach Mauricio Pochettino.
Ongoing stories, including the Brooklyn building collapse and the Ukraine talks, carry their original and updated dates.

Items described as scheduled, planned or reported — including Pochettino’s appointment, exhibitions and events that have not yet opened, and China’s COP33 decision, which rests on unnamed sources — are not presented as completed or officially confirmed.

This edition has photos on the lead and on 18 of 23 other stories, using only Wikimedia Commons or U.S. government public-domain files, each credited and labelled as a file photo. None shows the events described.
Stories by region: U.S. 5, Canada 5, Hong Kong 5, China 4, World 5. China has four stories this morning rather than padding to five.
provenance: Stories are compiled from the linked sources; labels describe the type of claim each story rests on.
Source pages were opened during this morning’s research between about 6:20 and 6:40 AM ET; each check time is the logged time that page was fetched.

China Daily and Xinhua items are labelled State media; RTHK is Hong Kong’s public broadcaster and Anadolu Agency is Turkish state-run. Syntun’s Singles’ Day figures are a third-party industry estimate.

Some pages (including AP, Politico, the South China Morning Post and StreetInsider) returned access errors to automated fetches; those are access limits, not evidence that the reporting is wrong. Reuters’ Singles’ Day report was read in a StreetInsider republication through a web reader.
Where outlets gave different figures — the Nasser Hospital injury count (27 per the UN, about 30 per the BBC) and the size of the Chiapas migrant caravan — the edition states both.

stories.headline: Microsoft’s global outage runs into a second day, with Outlook still unreliable for many users
stories.deck: A Microsoft outage that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday was still disrupting Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services early Friday. Microsoft said it saw no sign of malicious activity and reported gradual, uneven recovery.
stories.summary: A Microsoft outage that began shortly before 1 p.m. ET on Thursday was still disrupting Outlook and other Microsoft 365 services early Friday. Microsoft said it saw no sign of malicious activity and reported gradual, uneven recovery. CNBC said Outlook, Teams and Microsoft 365 services such as SharePoint and Copilot were hit, along with outside services that connect to Outlook Calendar. In an update at about 5 a.m. ET Friday, Microsoft said users might still be unable to connect to several Microsoft 365 products, including Outlook on the web and desktop, and gave no timeline for full service; most access to Teams had returned. The company initially linked the problem to elevated load after a number of servers became unexpectedly unavailable, and said the failed automated health checks may originate from a specific component that processes server health. It said it was bringing affected systems back in stages and extending the retry window for delayed emails to up to 48 hours. The Guardian’s live coverage said Microsoft later reported “positive results for server stability” after a software patch but still listed service degradation, and that government agencies in Australia, Japan and the United States were among those affected. The Canadian Press said thousands in Canada were affected. Microsoft shares were 2.6% lower in premarket trading, CNBC said.
stories.why: Outlook and Teams sit under the email, calendars and classes of millions of schools, offices and governments, so a two-day outage shows how much daily life now depends on a single company’s cloud — and how slowly that kind of failure can be fixed.
stories.label: Reported + company statement
stories.note: Microsoft’s explanation of the cause is its own preliminary account. Recovery was still in progress when this edition was compiled; service may differ by region and account.

stories.headline: Trump says the U.S. doesn’t need a deal with Iran and pulls Vance off the negotiations
stories.summary: President Donald Trump said Thursday that the United States no longer needs a deal with Iran and that he had asked Vice President JD Vance to turn his “complete and total attention” to alleged crime and corruption in Democratic-run cities and states instead of the Iran talks. “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” he wrote on Truth Social, referring to the Strait of Hormuz. NBC News noted that before the Nov. 3 midterms Trump had repeatedly said a deal could come soon. The Wall Street Journal had reported that Vance reached out to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, and was weighing direct talks, NBC and USA Today said. Vance said after the elections that voter anger over the war was the “real reason” Republicans lost. USA Today said the conflict began in February with U.S. airstrikes and has killed 23 U.S. service members, and that Trump said on Nov. 9 that escalation “won’t be necessary” and that the naval blockade and sanctions would stay in place.
stories.why: Shutting down the main diplomatic track points to an open-ended standoff in the Gulf, with consequences for oil and gas prices, and it sidelines the vice president who had blamed the war for the midterm defeat.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + claim
stories.note: Trump’s statements about seized Iranian money and control of the Strait are his claims. The Wall Street Journal reporting on Vance’s outreach is relayed by NBC News and USA Today.

stories.headline: Chris Van Hollen launches a challenge to Chuck Schumer for Senate Democratic leader
stories.summary: Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland announced Thursday that he will run for Senate majority leader, becoming the first Democrat to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York, who has led the caucus since 2017, NBC News reported. “In this election, the American people called for change… It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said in a statement. Democrats won control of the Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms. NBC said Schumer remains favored, and that Democratic senators will choose their leaders for the next Congress in a closed-door vote in December that requires a simple majority. Van Hollen told MS NOW on Thursday night that more than 10 senators had pledged to support him and called himself “the underdog.”
stories.why: Whoever leads the new Democratic majority will set the Senate’s agenda against President Trump for the next two years, so the contest is an early test of whether the party’s midterm win brings new leadership or continuity.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + claim
stories.note: The count of senators backing Van Hollen is his own claim and has not been confirmed.

stories.headline: Brooklyn collapse inquiry turns to the construction site next door, where city records show orders were ignored
stories.summary: With rescue work over, the investigation into Wednesday’s collapse of a three-storey apartment building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue, which killed eight people, has turned to the excavation next door at 2625 Bedford Avenue. Gothamist reported that Department of Buildings records show the project had ignored the agency’s orders earlier this year: a stop-work order was issued in March during demolition of a one-storey building after contractors failed to install required safety measures such as netting and sheds, and a month later an inspector found demolition had continued in violation of the order and issued another penalty. Structural plans filed for the new building called for shoring, vibration monitors and crack gauges on neighbouring buildings; Gothamist said it was unclear whether those precautions were taken, and the department says the cause is still under investigation. Mayor Zohran Mamdani said five main entities involved in the site are associated with about 100 other sites across the city and that inspectors had begun sweeps of them. The FDNY said its operations ended at 3:37 p.m. Thursday and the site was handed to the Department of Buildings and the NYPD, News 12 reported. Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez has said prosecutors are examining whether any criminal conduct contributed.
stories.why: Brooklyn is full of excavations beside older buildings, so what investigators find about the safeguards at this site — and at the roughly 100 related sites — matters to neighbours across the borough.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Ongoing story, first reported in the Nov 12 editions. No cause has been officially determined, and no one has been charged. The developer did not respond to Gothamist’s calls.

stories.headline: Commanders beat the Giants 24-21 on a late Diggs touchdown at MetLife Stadium
stories.summary: The Washington Commanders beat the New York Giants 24-21 on Thursday Night Football at MetLife Stadium when Stefon Diggs caught a 32-yard touchdown pass from Jayden Daniels with 57 seconds left. The Giants had gone ahead by four midway through the fourth quarter on J.J. McCarthy’s 66-yard touchdown pass to tight end Isaiah Likely, and safeties Jevón Holland and Ar’Darius Washington then intercepted Daniels on back-to-back drives, but New York went three-and-out after each turnover, the team’s website said. McCarthy threw for a career-high 293 yards and Cam Skattebo ran for 78 yards and two touchdowns. The Giants (5-3-1) still lead the NFC East but lost their first division game; Washington improved to 3-5-1. “It’s a missed opportunity,” coach John Harbaugh said. The Giants host Jacksonville next, in a game the NFL moved to a 4:25 p.m. kickoff.
stories.why: Two squandered turnovers let a struggling division rival back in, and the loss tightens the NFC East race for a Giants team that had looked in control.
stories.label: Reported

stories.headline: McGill researchers find a deepfake network using stolen influencers’ faces to spread trade-war falsehoods to Canadians
stories.summary: Researchers at McGill University’s Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy said Thursday they had found a network of at least 293 TikTok and Instagram accounts that take real creators’ videos and use AI to redraw their lips and add synthetic voices, making them appear to talk about Canadian politics. Between Aug. 7 and Nov. 4 the accounts posted 3,201 videos with 22.1 million plays, much of it about the U.S.–Canada trade war and Alberta’s referendum. One false story — a non-existent 48-hour ultimatum from President Donald Trump, to which Prime Minister Mark Carney supposedly responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts — was shared in 161 videos and played 5.1 million times, the report said. TikTok labelled only 4% of the videos as AI, and only 6.3% of commenters flagged them as fake. The researchers said the network is “almost certainly” run from outside North America; some accounts carry Chinese-language settings or a registration in China, which they called “the only lead we have on a country.” They said it does not push any government’s line and has not been monetized, and its purpose is unclear.
stories.why: Fakes built from real people’s faces are harder for platforms and viewers to spot, and this network targeted exactly the issues — trade, tariffs, Alberta — on which Canadians are making political decisions.
stories.label: Reported + analysis
stories.note: The origin and purpose assessments are the researchers’ own analysis; they say who runs the network is not known.

stories.headline: U.S. trade chief Greer says Canada and the U.S. have discussed a deal in recent days, but sets no deadline
stories.summary: U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Thursday that Canadian and American officials have discussed a trade deal within the past few days, but would not commit to a timeline, The Hub reported from his interview on CNBC’s Squawk Pod. “The substance of the deal is more important than a timeline,” he said, adding that President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney speak regularly. Ottawa wants a return to unfettered cross-border trade, Greer said, while Washington’s priority is protecting American supply chains. The Hub noted that talks collapsed in August; on Aug. 22 Washington imposed 50% tariffs on roughly US$20 billion in Canadian goods, Ottawa answered with counter-tariffs from Sept. 8, and Trump has threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel from Jan. 1, 2027. Greer said the administration is “going to keep taking trade actions as necessary.”
stories.why: With Democrats taking over Congress in January and tariffs blamed for higher prices, any sign that talks have restarted matters for Canadian jobs in autos, dairy and steel — but Greer’s words commit Washington to nothing.
stories.label: Reported + official statement
stories.note: Greer’s remarks are relayed by The Hub from a CNBC interview; this edition did not hear the interview directly.

stories.headline: Carney leaves Dublin talks on Ukraine and Europe for the ASEAN summit in Manila, with a Xi meeting planned later
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney wrapped up the European Political Community summit in Dublin on Thursday, where Canada was again the only non-European country at the table, and is heading to the ASEAN summit in Manila. In Dublin, Carney heard from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on the talks with Russia and said security guarantees for Ukraine are “a European responsibility, with Canada, with the United States,” in tiers, CBC News reported. His office said he met the leaders of Cyprus, Denmark, France, Greece, Ireland, Latvia and Sweden; CBC said he pressed Greece and Cyprus, which have not ratified Canada’s trade deal with the EU. The Canadian Press said the Rohingya refugee crisis is expected to be a major topic in Manila. CBC said the trip ends at the APEC leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, where a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping is planned.
stories.why: Carney is trying to build trade and security ties beyond the United States, and the stops in Europe, Southeast Asia and China show how widely Ottawa is now hedging.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: Rapper Shad returns to London, Ont., as Museum London’s first musician-in-residence
stories.summary: Juno-winning rapper Shad (Shadrach Kabango) has become Museum London’s first musician-in-residence, a year-long program in the Ontario city where he grew up and first fell in love with music, CBC News reported. The residency was set to launch Thursday evening with a conversation with broadcaster Garvia Bailey. Shad told CBC that memory will be a big theme — his own memories of London’s record stores and early freestyling, and the museum’s work preserving the community’s past. His projects include curating playlists inspired by the museum’s programming and moments in the city’s history, starting with one marking London’s bicentennial.
stories.why: Museums bringing in working musicians is a small but growing way to draw younger audiences, and it gives one of Canada’s most respected rappers a platform at home.

stories.headline: Alberta doctors and nurses question a push to discharge hospital patients by 11 a.m.
stories.summary: Alberta Health Services is encouraging hospitals to discharge patients by 11 a.m., and some doctors and nurses say the target could backfire, CBC News reported. Dr. Greg Hrynchyshyn of the Alberta Medical Association said an internal memo set a goal of discharging 40% of patients by that time, and asked whether patients who can’t be discharged before 11 might be held to the next day to meet “an artificial metric.” Danielle Larivee of United Nurses of Alberta said “it’s not like a hotel.” AHS says the initiative gives families more time to arrange medications and transport and improves patient flow, and that “patients will never be rushed to leave.”
stories.why: Hospital crowding is one of Alberta’s biggest public-service problems, and the dispute shows how a simple efficiency target can collide with clinical judgment.
stories.label: Reported + official statement

stories.headline: Sogo says a breach may have exposed data of about 820,000 members; Chow Sang Sang also reports unauthorised access
stories.summary: Department store Sogo Hong Kong said unauthorised parties had obtained some data from its membership system, and the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data said the incident may affect about 820,000 members. The privacy office said it received Sogo’s notification on Thursday, that Sogo found abnormal data-reading records on Nov. 5, and that the data may include names, email addresses, phone numbers and points balances; it has opened an investigation. Separately, jeweller Chow Sang Sang said it found unauthorised access to parts of its systems on Wednesday that may involve customers’ names, contact details, some order details and the last four digits of credit card numbers, as well as employee data, The Standard reported. Both companies urged customers to beware of calls or messages impersonating them.
stories.why: Two big retailers reporting breaches in one day means hundreds of thousands of Hong Kong shoppers face a higher risk of convincing phishing scams that use their real names and purchase details.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + company statement

stories.headline: Queen Mary Hospital lift faults: government report blames contractors and lax supervision, including by its own staff
stories.summary: Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn told a special Legislative Council panel meeting on Friday (Hong Kong time) that the main contractor and the lift subcontractor bear the main responsibility for faults in the lifts at Queen Mary Hospital’s new clinical block, RTHK reported. She said their work was inaccurate and poorly done, that an inspection and testing plan had omissions no one followed up, and that Architectural Services Department staff were negligent in issuing a completion certificate, with shortcomings too in how the Electrical and Mechanical Services Department issues lift permits. She said the supervision system itself is sound and the problem lay in execution. Faults among the block’s 28 lifts have delayed its full opening. DAB lawmaker Chan Hok-fung called it a “perfect storm”; Liberal Party lawmaker Lee Chun-keung said it “looks very much like a deliberate, chain-by-chain cover-up.”
stories.why: The new block is meant to expand one of Hong Kong’s main public hospitals, and the findings raise questions about how government checks public works.
stories.label: Official statement + reported + allegation
stories.note: Lee’s cover-up remark is a lawmaker’s allegation, not a finding of the report.

stories.headline: Hong Kong police arrest 10 over fake concert tickets sold at half price and handed over at MTR stations
stories.summary: Hong Kong police said Thursday they had arrested 10 people, aged 18 to 46, in a two-day operation against fake concert tickets and money laundering, after finding mule accounts linked to the cases had handled more than HK$81 million in suspected crime proceeds. They were arrested on suspicion of conspiracy to defraud, obtaining property by deception and money laundering. Police said sellers advertised tickets on social media at half price a day or two before shows, then met buyers at MTR stations and even “demonstrated” how to check a ticket before disappearing; victims found out only at the venue gate. The Standard said the accounts were also linked to at least 12 fraud cases with losses of more than HK$360,000. Police said genuine tickets have smooth paper, a reflective laser sticker and invisible fluorescent ink, and urged people to buy only through official channels.
stories.why: With a busy run of big concerts in Hong Kong, last-minute resale is where fans are most exposed — and police say the fakes are hard to spot by eye.
stories.label: Official statement + allegation
stories.note: Those arrested have not been convicted; the case details are police allegations.

stories.headline: Housing Authority lets families with young children borrow up to 95% for subsidised flats and shortens a resale ban
stories.summary: Hong Kong’s Housing Authority on Friday approved two changes to help people buy subsidised sale flats, RTHK reported. From the next Home Ownership Scheme sale, the maximum mortgage loan-to-value ratio for White Form family applicants with newborns will rise from 90% to 95%, and all families with children aged three or under by the application deadline will qualify. The authority also cut the resale restriction period for subsidised flats first offered between 2022 and 2025 from 15 years to 10. A spokesman said the measures would help more families move up the housing ladder and increase turnover of subsidised flats.
stories.why: A smaller down payment can decide whether a young family can afford a first flat in one of the world’s most expensive housing markets.

stories.summary: The Hong Kong government gazetted the Centre for Medical Products Regulation Bill on Friday, which would give the Centre for Medical Products Regulation statutory status and bring the regulation of Chinese and Western medicines and medical devices under one framework, according to a government press release. The bill would set the centre up as a body corporate to represent “Hong Kong, China” in international regulatory affairs. Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau said the aim is to approve advanced medical products more quickly and, in the long run, to make the centre an internationally recognised regulator. The bill is to be introduced into the Legislative Council.
stories.why: A faster, internationally recognised approval system could speed new drugs and devices to Hong Kong patients and support the city’s push to become a medical-innovation hub.

CBC News has reported that Prime Minister Mark Carney also plans to meet Xi in Shenzhen.

stories.headline: China rules out hosting the 2028 COP33 climate summit, the Guardian reports
stories.summary: China has decided not to host the COP33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberation, the Guardian reported Thursday, leaving the Asia-Pacific slot open to other countries. Bloomberg later reported the same, citing people familiar with the matter, Lianhe Zaobao said. The reasons were not given; experts who spoke to the Guardian suggested the U.S. election cycle was likely a factor, noting that the next U.S. presidential election, on Nov. 7, 2028, falls close to the start of that year’s summit, as Climate Home News also observed. The Chinese delegation at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, did not immediately respond to requests for comment, Zaobao said. Climate Home News said Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand have been mentioned as possible hosts; Zaobao said no country has made a formal bid since India withdrew in April. The 2028 summit is due to conclude the next global review of progress under the Paris Agreement.
stories.why: Many had hoped the world’s biggest emitter — and now the leading clean-energy manufacturer — would take the lead on climate diplomacy while Washington steps back, so Beijing’s choice leaves a key year without an obvious champion.
stories.label: Reported + unnamed sources
stories.note: China has not announced the decision publicly; the reports rest on unnamed sources.

stories.headline: China’s Singles’ Day sales grow 4.8% to 1.78 trillion yuan, a third-party tally shows, far slower than last year
stories.summary: Sales during China’s weeks-long Singles’ Day shopping festival, from Oct. 7 to Nov. 11, reached 1,776.4 billion yuan (about US$264 billion by Syntun’s conversion; Reuters put it at $267 billion) across online platforms, data provider Syntun said Thursday. E-commerce platforms accounted for 1,679.0 billion yuan, with Tmall ranked first; instant retail and community group-buying added 89.1 billion and 8.3 billion yuan. Reuters, citing Syntun, said that was up 4.8% from a year earlier, compared with 14.2% growth in last year’s festival, against a backdrop of weak consumer confidence. Alibaba and JD.com no longer publish headline sales totals; JD said it sold more than 50 million AI-related products, and platforms leaned on AI shopping assistants, Reuters said.
stories.why: Singles’ Day is one of the few broad readings of Chinese consumer spending, and slower growth fits the picture of cautious households that Beijing is trying to coax into spending more.
stories.label: Industry figures + reported
stories.note: Syntun’s figures are a third-party estimate; the platforms do not publish comparable totals. Dollar conversions differ slightly by source.

stories.headline: Kremlin says it has not yet agreed to Europeans at the Ukraine talks, as both sides report heavy overnight strikes
stories.summary: A day after U.S. envoy Jared Kushner said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to bring European countries into the next round of peace talks, the Kremlin said Friday it had not yet agreed to include European mediators. “Once we understand their real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, Al Jazeera reported. Kushner wrote on X that the expanded talks would address “broader postwar European security arrangements” alongside territorial issues, and that the sides were working toward “the largest prisoner exchange of the war,” the Guardian reported; Putin, meeting the envoys Thursday, refused to soften his territorial demands and warned against European peacekeepers. Fighting continued overnight: Russia’s defence ministry said it intercepted 1,198 Ukrainian drones over more than 15 regions, and the Volgograd governor said four people were killed, while in Ukraine a hospital in Kyiv caught fire after a Russian drone strike and Odesa’s military administration said at least two people were killed in attacks on the port city. EU leaders meeting in Dublin on Friday — at a summit originally meant to focus on artificial intelligence — were trying to settle who should speak for Europe, Euronews reported.
stories.why: Whether Europe gets a seat — and who fills it — will shape any settlement’s security terms, and the overnight strikes show the fighting is not pausing for diplomacy.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + claim
stories.note: Ongoing story: the Nov 12 Evening Edition covered the envoys’ meetings with Putin and Zelenskyy. Casualty and drone figures are each side’s own claims and could not be independently confirmed.

stories.headline: Israeli strike on Gaza’s Nasser Hospital kills six, including a surgeon, health officials say
stories.summary: An Israeli air strike on the surgical building of Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, the largest hospital in southern Gaza, killed six people overnight into Thursday, including surgeon Dr. Rizq Abu Shaira, according to Gaza’s Hamas-run health ministry, the BBC reported. The UN put the injured at 27; the BBC said about 30. The Israeli military said it targeted a commander of Hamas’s armed wing and other fighters who had used the hospital as a “headquarters”; Hamas called that a false narrative. Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s acting Middle East peace coordinator, said he was deeply alarmed and that the violence jeopardises the “increasingly fragile ceasefire.” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said health facilities must never be militarised or attacked; WHO has documented more than 1,000 attacks on health care in Gaza since October 2023. The UN said about 1.4 million people are living in tents or makeshift shelters as winter sets in.
stories.why: Strikes on Gaza’s few working hospitals test a ceasefire that is already fraying, and Israel’s ban on foreign reporters makes it hard to establish what happened.
stories.label: Reported + official statement + claim
stories.note: Casualty figures differ between sources. Israel’s and Hamas’s accounts of the target are their own claims; Israel does not allow international news organisations into Gaza, the BBC noted.

stories.headline: Trump threatens to double tariffs on Mexico over migrant caravans; Sheinbaum says none has reached the U.S. border
stories.summary: President Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday morning that “huge caravans” were forming and moving through Mexico and that if Mexico did not stop them, “the Tariffs on Mexico will be IMMEDIATELY DOUBLED,” Fox News reported. At her morning news conference, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said no migrant caravan had reached the northern border since Trump returned to office. She said there were currently two caravans: one that formed in Arriaga, Chiapas, with 500 to 600 people, of whom fewer than 100 remain, and a second, mostly Honduran group, which Courthouse News put at about 1,500 people. She said migrants receive humanitarian assistance and most return home once they learn they cannot cross into the U.S. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin wrote that the caravan “will NOT be allowed to enter our country.” Trump’s post linked the caravans to Republicans’ midterm losses.
stories.why: A doubling of tariffs would hit one of America’s largest trading relationships, and the threat shows Trump is still using trade penalties as leverage on migration after his party’s midterm defeat.

stories.headline: Manchester United agree deal to make USA coach Mauricio Pochettino their new manager, reports say
stories.summary: Manchester United have agreed a deal for Mauricio Pochettino, the U.S. men’s national team head coach, to replace Michael Carrick, who was sacked on Thursday with the club in the Premier League relegation zone, Sky Sports reported. Sky and Ireland’s RTÉ said he is expected to sign a two-and-a-half-year contract, until 2029, and that a formal announcement could come as early as Friday. Both said Pochettino would first take charge of the USA’s Nations League quarter-final matches against Haiti on Saturday and Tuesday before heading to Manchester; United’s next match is against Liverpool on Nov. 22. RTÉ, citing reports, said U.S. Soccer would receive $10 million in compensation plus $2 million for his coaching staff. Pochettino signed an extension with U.S. Soccer through 2030 only three months ago, RTÉ noted.
stories.why: The move would cost the U.S. its head coach early in the build-up to the 2030 World Cup, while United bet on a proven Premier League manager to escape a relegation fight.

stories.headline: A bronze leg found in a Scottish bog anchors Edinburgh’s biggest-ever exhibition on Roman Scotland
stories.summary: A gilded bronze leg dug out of a bog in the Scottish Borders in 1820 — long thought to have been looted from England and carried north by raiding tribes — is now believed to have come from a huge statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius on horseback erected near Hawick around AD 140, the Guardian reported. It is the centrepiece of “Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire,” which the Guardian describes as the largest exhibition ever staged on the Romans in Scotland; it opens Saturday at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. Principal curator Fraser Hunter argues the Romans were a far bigger force north of Hadrian’s Wall than once thought. The show also includes a reconstructed decorated bowl and two altars from the Mithras temple at the Roman fort at Inveresk, east of Edinburgh, according to the museum.
stories.why: It recasts a familiar story — that Rome stopped at Hadrian’s Wall — and shows how new research on old finds can change national history.
stories.label: Reported + analysis
stories.note: The statue identification is the curators’ interpretation.
